There are a lot of intermarriages between Nubi and non-Nubi. The persons who enter the Nubi community do also learn the language. In Bombo, Uganda, I have met women who married Nubi and then learnt Kinubi.
According to some local sources, Kinubi may also be used as a lingua franca by non-Nubi in some areas of Uganda, but is is mainly spoken as a creole.

Kinubi tends to be spoken less among the young generation in cities like Mombasa in Kenya or Kampala in Uganda, and more stable in smaller cities like Bombo, Uganda. In both countries, the Muslims - all Nubi are Muslims - have a stong feeling of identification with Swahili culture and language, which is also widespread outside the Muslim community.In Tanzania, it seems that all the former Kinubi speakers now speak Swahili.
The language seems to have disappeared in Tanzania and in Somalia, but is still spoken in Uganda and Kenya.
There is no official data, but the language is spoken in many places in Uganda and Kenya, as well as in Sudan, so we may imagine that there are some hundreds of thousands of speakers.
In Uganda, some interviews were done about Nubi culture and broadcast on radio. However, Kinubi is not used on a regular basis in this context.
Kinubi is used in music in the Nubi community, at least in Kenya, Uganda and even Sudan. I personnally recorded some songs in Bombo, Uganda.
Some individuals write in Kinubi: Mustapher Khamisy in Bombo writes poems in Kinubi and distributes them during Nubi parties, weddings, etc.
Wellens (2005) sees a difference in stress: Wedé is the attributive demonstrative and wéde the independent demonstrative.
Kinubi is not used as the medium of instruction in school, but it may be used in religious schools related to mosques, at least in Uganda.
Young Nubi exchange emails in various languages, including Kinubi. (In addition, they  use  English and Swahili, sometimes even a mixture of the three languages.)
Both Swahili and English have a strong influence on the language (e.g. code-switching, borrowings).
Some phonological features play a role in distinguishing Ugandan and Kenyan Kinubi: some phonemes are more stable in Mombasa, free variation for some consonants is more common in Uganda.
Some features play a role in distinguishing Ugandan and Kenyan Kinubi. One such feature is neagtion: it is mainly postverbal in Uganda and preverbal in Kenya.
Some words differ: 'clothes' is said lidim in Mombasa and gumas in Bombo, 'room' is chumba in Mombasa and kujura in Bombo.
Besides de and nade, there is another form, used by some few informants: dak 'that'.
